claim: Examining a world-wide panel of 316 genetically distinct C. elegans wild strains, highly variable average egg number in utero (a proxy for egg retention) in self-fertilizing adult hermaphrodites (mid-L4 +48 hr) was found, ranging from approximately 5–50 eggs retained in utero.
source: Examining a world-wide panel of 316 genetically distinct C. elegans wild strains, we found highly variable average egg number in utero (a proxy for egg retention) in self-fertilizing adult hermaphrodites (mid-L4 +48 hr), ranging from approximately 5–50 eggs retained in utero (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data presented in Figure 1A-C showing measurements of egg retention across 316 strains.

claim: Most C. elegans strains (81%, N=256) differed relatively subtly in the number of eggs in utero (Class II canonical egg retention: 10–25 eggs).
source: To simplify further analysis of natural variation in egg retention, we defined three phenotypic classes: most strains (81%, N=256) differed relatively subtly in the number of eggs in utero (Class II canonical egg retention: 10–25 eggs), including the laboratory reference strain N2.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from the analysis of 316 strains, with specific percentages and sample sizes provided.

claim: A small number of C. elegans strains consistently showed strongly reduced egg retention (Class I weak egg retention: <10 eggs, 15%, N=46).
source: A small number of strains consistently showed either strongly reduced (Class I weak egg retention:<10 eggs, 15%, N=46) or increased egg retention (Class III: strong egg retention:>25 eggs or larvae in utero, 4%, N=14).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from the analysis of 316 strains, with specific percentages and sample sizes provided.

claim: A small number of C. elegans strains consistently showed increased egg retention (Class III: strong egg retention: >25 eggs or larvae in utero, 4%, N=14).
source: A small number of strains consistently showed either strongly reduced (Class I weak egg retention:<10 eggs, 15%, N=46) or increased egg retention (Class III: strong egg retention:>25 eggs or larvae in utero, 4%, N=14).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from the analysis of 316 strains, with specific percentages and sample sizes provided.

claim: Several Class III C. elegans strains exhibited internal hatching.
source: Several Class III strains also exhibited internal hatching (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data referenced in the source data file.

claim: No obvious evidence was found for relationships between natural variation in C. elegans egg retention and geographical and climatic parameters (e.g. latitude/longitude, elevation).
source: To examine if natural variation in egg retention may be linked to strain differences in ecological niche, we tested for effects of geographical and climatic parameters (e.g. latitude/longitude, elevation) (Spearman rank correlations, all p>0.05; data not shown) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and substrate type (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) on mean egg retention but found no obvious evidence for such relationships.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analyses (Spearman rank correlations) showing no significant relationships.

claim: No obvious evidence was found for relationships between natural variation in C. elegans egg retention and substrate type.
source: To examine if natural variation in egg retention may be linked to strain differences in ecological niche, we tested for effects of geographical and climatic parameters (e.g. latitude/longitude, elevation) (Spearman rank correlations, all p>0.05; data not shown) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and substrate type (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) on mean egg retention but found no obvious evidence for such relationships.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing no clear patterns.

claim: Strains of all three phenotypic Classes were found across the globe and may co-occur in the same locality, or even in the same microhabitat or substrate.
source: Strains of all three phenotypic Classes were found across the globe and may co-occur in the same locality, or even in the same microhabitat or substrate (Figure 1—source data 1), as previously reported (Vigne et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 1—source data 1 and is corroborated by a previous publication (Vigne et al., 2021).

claim: A majority (11 out of 14) of Class III strains were isolated in Europe.
source: A majority (11 out of 14) of Class III strains were isolated in Europe (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but this may be simply due to increased sampling efforts of this region.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GWA mapping using data for 316 unique strains (isotypes) for mean egg retention yielded a single QTL located on chromosome III spanning 1.48 Mb.
source: Performing GWA mapping using data for 316 unique strains (isotypes), mapping of mean egg retention yielded a single QTL located on chromosome III spanning 1.48 Mb (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GWA mapping results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The QTL on chromosome III for mean egg retention explained 24% of the observed phenotypic variance.
source: This QTL explained 24% of the observed phenotypic variance (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Table 1.

claim: Among the 257 genes found in the QTL region on chromosome III, five have known roles in the egg-laying system.
source: Among the 257 genes found in this QTL region, five have known roles in the egg-laying system (https://www.wormbase.org) and display various natural polymorphisms (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Table 2 and draws on established knowledge from WormBase.

claim: No obvious candidate polymorphisms were detected in the five genes with known roles in egg-laying within the QTL region that could explain variable levels of egg retention.
source: However, we did not detect any obvious candidate polymorphisms in these genes that could explain variable levels of egg retention.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of genetic variants in candidate genes within the QTL region.

claim: Two additional QTL on chromosomes II and IV were detected for variance in egg retention (CV).
source: Two additional QTL on chromosomes II and IV were detected for variance in egg retention (CV) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by GWA mapping results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The three QTLs detected for egg retention do not align with any of the recently identified hyper-divergent regions of the C. elegans genome.
source: The three QTLs do not align with any of the recently identified hyper-divergent regions of the genome (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previously published genomic data (Lee et al., 2021).

claim: Natural variation in C. elegans egg retention is likely polygenic, influenced by multiple common variants.
source: The phenotypic distributions and detection of several QTL by GWA indicates that natural variation in C. elegans egg retention is likely polygenic, influenced by multiple common variants.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the detection of multiple QTL and the phenotypic distribution patterns.

claim: Four C. elegans strains (including the newly isolated strain NIC1832) carry a single amino acid substitution (V530L) in KCNL-1.
source: Among the Class III strains with very strong egg retention, four strains (including the newly isolated strain NIC1832) are known to carry a single amino acid substitution (V530L) in KCNL-1 (Vigne et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic data and a previous publication (Vigne et al., 2021).

claim: The KCNL-1 V530L variant has been shown to strongly reduce egg-laying activity.
source: This variant has been shown to strongly reduce egg-laying activity (Vigne et al., 2021), thus explaining strong egg retention in these four French strains.
evidence: The claim is supported by a previous publication (Vigne et al., 2021).

claim: The KCNL-1 V530L variant is likely derived from a single mutational event, as inferred by local haplotype analysis of the genomic region surrounding kcnl-1.
source: As previously suggested (Vigne et al., 2021), we confirmed that the KCNL-1 V530L is likely derived from a single mutational event, as inferred by local haplotype analysis of the genomic region surrounding kcnl-1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by haplotype analysis shown in Figure 2C and corroborated by a previous publication (Vigne et al., 2021).

claim: In additional Class III strains which do not carry the KCNL-1 V530L variant (N=10), the derived state of constitutively high egg retention must be explained by alternative genetic variants.
source: In additional Class III strains, which do not carry this variant (N=10), the derived state of constitutively high egg retention must thus be explained by alternative genetic variants.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that these strains exhibit high egg retention but lack the known KCNL-1 V530L variant.

claim: Natural variation in C. elegans egg retention is shaped by both common variants and multiple rare variants, including KCNL-1 V530L, explaining extreme phenotypic divergence.
source: Therefore, natural variation in C. elegans egg retention is shaped by both common variants and multiple rare variants, including KCNL-1 V530L, explaining extreme phenotypic divergence.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined evidence of QTL mapping (common variants) and identification of rare variants like KCNL-1 V530L.

claim: The temporal dynamics of egg number in utero varied strongly across the hermaphrodite reproductive span in the 15 focal strains.
source: The temporal dynamics of egg number in utero varied strongly across the hermaphrodite reproductive span (Figure 3C), in line with progeny production and presumptive ovulation rates, coupled to the number of remaining self-sperm (Ward and Carrel, 1979; McCarter et al., 1997; Kosinski et al., 2005; McMullen et al., 2012; Large et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and is consistent with previously published findings on progeny production and ovulation rates.

claim: Towards the end of the reproductive period (between mid-L4 +48 hr to mid-L4 +72 hr), surviving animals in all phenotypic Classes showed strongly reduced offspring numbers in utero.
source: Towards the end of the reproductive period (between mid-L4 +48 hr to mid-L4 +72 hr), surviving animals in all phenotypic Classes showed strongly reduced offspring numbers in utero (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Increased egg number in utero was linked to prolonged intra-uterine embryonic development in the 15 focal strains.
source: Scoring the age distribution of progeny in utero of young (mid-L4 +30 hr) adult hermaphrodites confirmed that increased egg number in utero was linked to prolonged intra-uterine embryonic development (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data on embryonic age distribution shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At mid-L4 +30 hr, most Class III strains contained more advanced embryonic stages (or L1 larvae) compared to Class I and II strains.
source: At this developmental stage, most Class III strains contained more advanced embryonic stages (or L1 larvae) compared to Class I and II strains (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data on embryonic age distribution shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Internal hatching occurred consistently in the six strains with highest egg retention: all Class IIIB strains and in two Class IIIA strains (JU830, JU2829).
source: Examining the temporal dynamics of internal hatching across the entire reproductive span, we found that internal hatching occurred consistently in the six strains with highest egg retention: all Class IIIB strains and in two Class IIIA strains (JU830, JU2829; Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data on internal hatching shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Both egg and body size (of early adults at beginning of fertilization, containing 1–2 eggs in utero) showed significant differences across the 15 focal strains.
source: Both egg and body size (of early adults at beginning of fertilization, containing 1–2 eggs in utero) showed significant differences across strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C); in addition, there was a trend for a correlation between body and egg size across strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: There was a trend for a correlation between body and egg size across the 15 focal strains.
source: Both egg and body size (of early adults at beginning of fertilization, containing 1–2 eggs in utero) showed significant differences across strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C); in addition, there was a trend for a correlation between body and egg size across strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Egg and body size did not correlate with measures of mean egg retention across the 15 focal strains.
source: However, egg and body size did not correlate with measures of mean egg retention across strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F), suggesting that the capacity to retain eggs is not simply a function of body or egg size.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Egg-laying activity was highly dynamic, peaking between mid-L4 +24 hr and mid-L4 +30 hr for most strains, followed by a decline until cessation of reproduction.
source: In line with the temporal progression of egg retention (Figure 3C), egg-laying activity was highly dynamic, peaking between mid-L4 +24 hr and mid-L4 +30 hr for most strains, followed by a decline until cessation of reproduction (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data on egg-laying activity shown in Figure 4.

claim: Most Class III strains exhibited a shortened time window of egg-laying activity, with few eggs being laid from mid-L4 +48 hr onwards.
source: Most Class III strains exhibited a shortened time window of egg-laying activity, with few eggs being laid from mid-L4 +48 hr onwards (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data on egg-laying activity shown in Figure 4.

claim: The number of intervals with egg laying varied significantly between strains and Classes.
source: The number of intervals with egg laying varied significantly between strains and Classes (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Class I strains exhibited an increased number of intervals with egg laying.
source: In line with their egg retention phenotype, Class I strains exhibited an increased number of intervals with egg laying, whereas Class IIIB strains showed a reduced number of such intervals (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Class IIIB strains showed a reduced number of intervals with egg laying.
source: In line with their egg retention phenotype, Class I strains exhibited an increased number of intervals with egg laying, whereas Class IIIB strains showed a reduced number of such intervals (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The number of intervals with egg laying did not significantly differ between Class II and IIIA strains.
source: In contrast, the number of intervals with egg laying did not significantly differ between Class II and IIIA strains (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Strains with strong egg retention tended to exhibit prolonged periods during which egg laying was inactive.
source: Moreover, strains with strong egg retention tended to exhibit prolonged periods during which egg laying was inactive (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The reference strain N2 (Class II) expelled significantly more eggs per interval (with egg laying) compared to all other strains, including QX1430.
source: In addition, the reference strain N2 (Class II) expelled significantly more eggs per interval (with egg laying) compared to all other strains, including QX1430 – therefore, this atypical phenotype likely caused by the N2-specific npr-1 allele (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E and is inferred to be caused by the N2-specific npr-1 allele.

claim: Hermaphrodites of Class II strains laid their first egg after accumulating ~5–10 eggs in utero, that is approximately 1–2 hr after first fertilization.
source: Hermaphrodites of Class II strains laid their first egg after accumulating ~5–10 eggs in utero, that is approximately 1–2 hr after first fertilization, similar to what has been reported previously for the reference strain N2 (Ravi et al., 2018; Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and B and is consistent with previously published findings (Ravi et al., 2018).

claim: The time points of the first egg-laying event for Class I and III strains were significantly advanced and delayed, respectively, with corresponding differences in the number of eggs accumulated in utero.
source: By comparison, the time points of the first egg-laying event for Class I and III strains were significantly advanced and delayed, respectively, with corresponding differences in the number of eggs accumulated in utero (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Exposure to a high dose of serotonin (25 mM) generated a consistent increase in egg laying in both Class I and II strains.
source: We found exposure to a high dose of serotonin (25 mM) to generate a consistent increase in egg laying in both Class I and II strains (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Among the five Class IIIA strains without the kcnl-1 variant, serotonin stimulated egg laying in all strains except for JU2829, in which serotonin strongly inhibited egg laying as compared to basal egg laying in controls.
source: In contrast, responses were highly variable in Class III strains: among the five Class IIIA strains without the kcnl-1 variant, serotonin stimulated egg laying in all strains except for JU2829, in which serotonin strongly inhibited egg laying as compared to basal egg laying in controls (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Serotonin induced a much stronger egg-laying response in the strain ED3005 than in other Class IIIA strains with similar levels of egg retention.
source: In addition, serotonin induced a much stronger egg-laying response in the strain ED3005 than in other Class IIIA strains with similar levels of egg retention (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In Class IIIB strains carrying the KCNL-1 V530L variant allele, serotonin had no effect on, or a trend towards inhibiting, an already weak egg laying activity.
source: In Class IIIB strains carrying the KCNL-1 V530L variant allele, serotonin had no effect on, or a trend towards inhibiting, an already weak egg laying activity (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Strains within Classes I, II, and IIIA showed subtle but significative quantitative differences in the egg-laying response triggered by serotonin despite showing grossly similar egg-laying behaviour in control conditions.
source: Strains within Classes I, II, and IIIA further showed subtle but significative quantitative differences in the egg-laying response triggered by serotonin despite showing grossly similar egg-laying behaviour in control conditions (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The SSRI fluoxetine (Prozac) and the tricyclic antidepressant imipramine strongly stimulated egg-laying activity in all 15 focal strains.
source: As reported for the reference strain N2 (Dempsey et al., 2005), we find that the SSRI fluoxetine (Prozac) and the tricyclic antidepressant imipramine strongly stimulated egg-laying activity in all 15 focal strains, which only showed slight (although significant) quantitative differences in drug sensitivity (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and is consistent with previously published findings (Dempsey et al., 2005).

claim: Both fluoxetine and imipramine stimulated egg laying in the Class IIIB strains and the Class IIIA strain JU2829 for which exogenous serotonin either inhibited egg laying or had no effect on it.
source: Both drugs also stimulated egg laying in the Class IIIB strains and the Class IIIA strain JU2829 for which exogenous serotonin either inhibited egg laying or had no effect on it (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Serotonin had a negative effect on egg laying in JU1200KCNL-1 V530L, suggesting that altering vulval muscle excitability by means of KCNL-1 V530L was sufficient to abrogate positive but not negative serotonin inputs acting in the C. elegans egg-laying system.
source: Very similar to what we found for JU751 (Class IIIB), serotonin had a negative effect on egg laying in JU1200KCNL-1 V530L, suggesting that altering vulval muscle excitability by means of KCNL-1 V530L was indeed sufficient to abrogate positive but not negative serotonin inputs acting in the C. elegans egg-laying system (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C and is inferred from the comparison of strains with and without the KCNL-1 V530L variant.

claim: Both fluoxetine and imipramine stimulated egg laying in JU1200KCNL-1 V530L.
source: In addition, both fluoxetine and imipramine stimulated egg laying in JU1200KCNL-1 V530L (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), very similar to what we observed in JU751 and other Class IIIB strains (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7B.

claim: Introducing the canonical KCNL-1 sequence into JU751 (strain JU751KCNL-1 L530V) fully restores egg-laying responses as for the ones observed in JU1200.
source: In addition, introducing the canonical KCNL-1 sequence into JU751 (strain JU751KCNL-1 L530V) fully restores egg-laying responses as for the ones observed in JU1200 (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Variation in a single amino acid residue of KCNL-1 is sufficient to explain drastic differences in the C. elegans egg-laying system and its response to various neuromodulatory inputs.
source: These results thus further confirm that variation in a single amino acid residue of KCNL-1 is sufficient to explain drastic differences in the C. elegans egg-laying system and its response to various neuromodulatory inputs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of experiments manipulating the KCNL-1 variant.

claim: mod-5(n822) tended to increase basal egg-laying activity in liquid M9 buffer without food.
source: Consistent with past reports, we found that mod-5(n822) tended to increase basal egg-laying activity in liquid M9 buffer without food.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and is consistent with previously published findings.

claim: The effect of mod-5(n822) on egg-laying activity was genotype-dependent, and several strains did not show a significantly increased egg-laying response (Class I: JU3166, QG2873, Class IIIA: JU830, Class IIIB: JU751).
source: However, the size of this effect was genotype-dependent, and several strains did not show a significantly increased egg-laying response (Class I: JU3166, QG2873, Class IIIA: JU830, Class IIIB: JU751) (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The effect of mod-5 was quantitatively different for certain strains within the same phenotypic Class (Class II and Class IIIA), indicating that serotonin sensitivity of the egg laying system varies genetically despite generating similar behavioural outputs.
source: The effect of mod-5 was also quantitatively different for certain strains within the same phenotypic Class (Class II and Class IIIA), indicating that serotonin sensitivity of the egg laying system varies genetically despite generating similar behavioural outputs (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B and is inferred from the observed variation.

claim: Introducing the mutation mod-5(n822) did not further increase egg laying when wild strains were exposed to 25 mM serotonin (except for the strain ED3005), likely because egg-laying activity was already at its maximum at such a high dose of serotonin.
source: Introducing the mutation mod-5(n822) did not further increase egg laying when wild strains were exposed to 25 mM serotonin (except for the strain ED3005), likely because egg-laying activity was already at its maximum at such a high dose of serotonin (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and is inferred from the observation of maximal egg-laying activity.

claim: Exposure to a range of lower serotonin concentrations uncovered significant strain differences in sensitivity to exogenous serotonin and these effects of genetic background were further contingent on the presence of mod-5(lf).
source: In contrast, exposure to a range of lower serotonin concentrations uncovered significant strain differences in sensitivity to exogenous serotonin and these effects of genetic background were further contingent on the presence of mod-5(lf) (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, and Table 3.

claim: Low exogenous serotonin concentrations strongly stimulated egg laying in Class I strains and ED3005 (Class IIIA), and this stimulation was significantly amplified in the presence of mod-5(lf).
source: Low exogenous serotonin concentrations strongly stimulated egg laying in Class I strains and ED3005 (Class IIIA), and this stimulation was significantly amplified in the presence of mod-5(lf) (Figure 8C), consistent with the previously observed serotonin hypersensitivity of ED3005 (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C and is consistent with previously observed serotonin hypersensitivity of ED3005 (Figure 7B).

claim: In Class II strains, including N2, low exogenous serotonin only marginally increased egg-laying, and mod-5(lf) had little effect.
source: By contrast, in Class II strains, including N2, low exogenous serotonin only marginally increased egg-laying, and mod-5(lf) had little effect (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: C. elegans harbours natural variation in its genetic architecture affecting sensitivity to neuromodulatory inputs of the egg-laying circuit.
source: Hence, C. elegans harbours natural variation in its genetic architecture affecting sensitivity to neuromodulatory inputs of the egg-laying circuit.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed epistatic interactions between genetic background and mod-5(lf) on egg-laying responses to serotonin.

claim: Strains with stronger egg retention generally showed reduced lifetime self-fertility and reduced survival, with strongest reductions observed in Class IIIB strains.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, strains with stronger egg retention generally showed reduced lifetime self-fertility and reduced survival, with strongest reductions observed in Class IIIB strains (Figure 9A-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9A-C.

claim: Class III strains showed frequent internal hatching, with mothers dying prematurely, sometimes before the end of the reproductive span.
source: Class III strains showed frequent internal hatching, with mothers dying prematurely, sometimes before the end of the reproductive span (Figure 10A-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10A-C.

claim: Internal hatching in Class I and II strains was absent or occurred only in rare instances at the end of the reproductive period.
source: Internal hatching in Class I and II strains was absent or occurred only in rare instances at the end of the reproductive period (Figure 10C), similar to what has been previously observed for the strain N2 (Pickett and Kornfeld, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10C and is consistent with previously published findings (Pickett and Kornfeld, 2013).

claim: A fraction of adults in multiple Class III (but not Class I or II) strains had self-sperm remaining at the time of internal hatching.
source: First, a fraction of adults in multiple Class III (but not Class I or II) strains had self-sperm remaining at the time of internal hatching (Figure 11), confirming that internal hatching can indeed occur during the reproductive span, potentially disrupting self-fertilization.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11.

claim: In the Class IIIB strain JU2593, the total number of self-sperm greatly exceeded the number of lifetime progeny.
source: Consistent with this latter scenario, in the Class IIIB strain JU2593, the total number of self-sperm greatly exceeded the number of lifetime progeny (Figure 11—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Internally hatched larvae in live mothers with remaining self-sperm (limited to Class III strains) caused apparent physical damage to the maternal gonad and somatic tissues due to larval movement, sometimes disrupting the uterine wall.
source: Second, internally hatched larvae in live mothers with remaining self-sperm (limited to Class III strains) caused apparent physical damage to the maternal gonad and somatic tissues due to larval movement, sometimes disrupting the uterine wall (Figure 11—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Larval movement scattered sperm away from the uterine regions adjacent to spermathecae, which likely reduces fertilization efficacy as certain Class III strains had large numbers of unfertilized oocytes in the uterus before self-sperm was depleted.
source: Third, larval movement also appeared to scatter sperm away from the uterine regions adjacent to spermathecae, which likely reduces fertilization efficacy as certain Class III strains had large numbers of unfertilized oocytes in the uterus before self-sperm was depleted (Figure 11—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1C and D and is inferred from the observation of scattered sperm and unfertilized oocytes.

claim: Strong egg retention (and internal hatching) correlates with reduced self-fertility.
source: The above experiments show that strong egg retention (and internal hatching) correlates with reduced self-fertility (Figure 9C) and reduced maternal survival (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Strong egg retention (and internal hatching) correlates with reduced maternal survival.
source: The above experiments show that strong egg retention (and internal hatching) correlates with reduced self-fertility (Figure 9C) and reduced maternal survival (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Class IIIB strains exhibited the most drastic reduction in reproductive output, only using a fraction of available self-sperm.
source: Class IIIB strains exhibited the most drastic reduction in reproductive output, only using a fraction of available self-sperm.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data on self-fertility, survival, and sperm usage in Class IIIB strains.

claim: In Class IIIA strains (ED3005, JU440, NIC1786) internal hatching occurred mainly after reproduction had ceased, suggesting that strong egg retention has limited detrimental fitness effects in these strains.
source: In contrast, in Class IIIA strains (ED3005, JU440, NIC1786) internal hatching occurred mainly after reproduction had ceased (Figure 10C), suggesting that strong egg retention has limited detrimental fitness effects in these strains.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10C and is inferred from the timing of internal hatching.

claim: Strong egg retention reflects prolonged intra-uterine embryonic development, which results in laying of eggs holding advanced-stage embryos.
source: Strong egg retention reflects prolonged intra-uterine embryonic development (Figure 3D), which results in laying of eggs holding advanced-stage embryos, as confirmed by scoring the age distribution of embryos contained in eggs laid by young adults of the 15 focal wild strains (Figure 12A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 12A.

claim: Within laid eggs of Class I and II strains, embryos rarely exceeded the 26-cell stage, whilst in Class III, many embryos had started to differentiate, containing hundreds of cells, including late-stage embryos, sometimes close to hatching.
source: Within laid eggs of Class I and II strains, embryos rarely exceeded the 26-cell stage, whilst in Class III, many embryos had started to differentiate, containing hundreds of cells, including late-stage embryos, sometimes close to hatching (Figure 12A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 12A.

claim: Eggs of all Class IIIB strains and some Class IIIA strains hatched on average ~2–5 hours earlier compared to Class I and II strains.
source: First, comparing the average timing of larval hatching between the 15 focal strains with variable egg retention, we found that eggs of all Class IIIB strains and some Class IIIA strains hatched on average ~2–5 hours earlier compared to Class I and II strains (Figure 12B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: Many Class III strains with strong egg retention reached age at maturity (~2–6 hr) earlier than Class I and II strains, although some Class III strains did not maintain their initial head start in larval development.
source: Second, to test if earlier larval hatching indeed translates into corresponding earlier onset of reproductive maturity in the 15 focal strains, we measured the time interval between egg laying and reproductive maturity, defined as the onset of fertilization, that is by the presence of 1–2 eggs in utero. Although many Class III strains with strong egg retention reached age at maturity (~2–6 hr) earlier than Class I and II strains, some Class III strains did not maintain their initial head start in larval development (Figure 12C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 12C.

claim: Strains with prolonged egg retention benefit from a relatively shorter developmental time from laying to reproductive maturity, which might improve competitive ability.
source: Overall, these measurements confirm that strains with prolonged egg retention benefit from a relatively shorter developmental time from laying to reproductive maturity, which might improve competitive ability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data on hatching time and egg-to-adult developmental time.

claim: The KCNL-1 V530L variant performed significantly better in competition against a GFP-tester strain compared to JU1200WT.
source: Estimating adult population number and genotype frequencies relative to the GFP-tester strain 5 days after inoculation (around the time point of food exhaustion), the KCNL-1 V530L variant performed significantly better (Figure 12D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 12D.

claim: Strong egg retention can improve competitive ability in food-limited environments.
source: Given that the principal phenotypic effect of KCNL-1 V530L is reduced egg laying and consequently increased egg retention (Vigne et al., 2021), we conclude that strong egg retention can improve competitive ability in food-limited environments.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the competition experiment results and the known effect of KCNL-1 V530L on egg retention.

claim: In all five competition experiments, JU751 reached higher adult population sizes at the time of food exhaustion compared to strains isolated from the same habitat.
source: We then estimated adult population size and genotype frequencies 5 days after inoculation (around the time point of food exhaustion). In all five cases, JU751 reached higher adult population sizes at this stage (Figure 12E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 12E.

claim: Laying of advanced-stage embryos may enhance intraspecific competitive ability, particularly in scenarios where multiple genotypes compete for colonization and exploitation of limited, patchily distributed resources.
source: These experimental results offer preliminary evidence (bearing in mind that our analysis was primarily centered on a single genetic background) that laying of advanced-stage embryos may enhance intraspecific competitive ability, particularly in scenarios where multiple genotypes compete for colonization and exploitation of limited, patchily distributed resources.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the competition experiment results.

claim: Increased egg-to-adult developmental time has previously been shown to be disadvantageous for C. elegans population growth when analysing mutants with increased hermaphrodite sperm production.
source: Similar to our experiments, increased egg-to-adult developmental time has previously been shown to be disadvantageous for C. elegans population growth when analysing mutants with increased hermaphrodite sperm production, which incurs a cost as the onset of reproductive maturity will be delayed; thus, although these mutants have the potential to produce overall many more self-progeny, they will be rapidly outcompeted because of delayed maturity whenever resources are limited (Hodgkin and Barnes, 1991; Barker, 1992; Cutter, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by previously published findings (Hodgkin and Barnes, 1991; Barker, 1992; Cutter, 2004).

claim: Maternal features accelerating offspring development after oviposition can confer fitness benefits in ephemeral habitats with rapidly decaying resources.
source: Together with theoretical and experimental evidence in insects (Bakker, 1961; Mueller and Bitner, 2015; Horváth and Kalinka, 2018), these observations indicate that maternal features accelerating offspring development after oviposition can confer fitness benefits in ephemeral habitats with rapidly decaying resources.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined evidence from the current study and previously published findings in insects (Bakker, 1961; Mueller and Bitner, 2015; Horváth and Kalinka, 2018).

claim: Across strains, most eggs removed from mothers and directly exposed to high concentrations of ethanol and acetic acid were killed, whereas eggs inside mothers exhibited significantly higher survival in most strains, particularly when exposed to acetic acid.
source: Across strains, most eggs removed from mothers and directly exposed to these chemical treatments were killed, whereas eggs inside mothers exhibited significantly higher survival in most strains, particularly when exposed to acetic acid (Figure 13A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 13A and B.

claim: Increased egg retention resulted in overall higher numbers of surviving offspring per mother in both ethanol and acetic acid stress treatments.
source: Consequently, increased egg retention resulted in overall higher numbers of surviving offspring per mother in both stress treatments (Figure 13A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 13A and B.

claim: Exposure to acetic acid confirmed that higher egg retention of JU751 increased the number of surviving offspring compared to strains with lower retention.
source: Exposure to acetic acid confirmed that higher egg retention of JU751 increased the number of surviving offspring compared to strains with lower retention (Figure 14A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 14A.

claim: The number of surviving offspring in the Class II strain JU1200WT (~15 eggs in utero) was much reduced compared to JU1200KCNL-1 V530L (~40 eggs in utero) when exposed to acetic acid.
source: In the same fashion, we found the number of surviving offspring in the Class II strain JU1200WT (~15 eggs in utero) to be much reduced compared to JU1200KCNL-1 V530L (~40 eggs in utero) when exposed to acetic acid (Figure 14B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 14B.

claim: Larvae in utero present at the time of acetic acid treatment were efficiently protected.
source: In addition, larvae in utero present at the time of treatment were also efficiently protected (Figure 14C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 14C.

claim: Fertility of individuals derived from stress-exposed eggs ex utero was reduced compared to the ones derived from eggs in utero when exposed to osmotic stress (15-hr exposure to 0.3 M NaCl).
source: We then followed surviving individuals to score their lifetime reproductive success under selfing. We found that fertility of individuals derived from stress-exposed eggs ex utero was reduced compared to the ones derived from eggs in utero (Figure 15B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 15B.

claim: Individuals derived from ex utero eggs exposed to a low concentration of acetic acid (1 M) developed more slowly and exhibited significantly delayed reproductive maturity (but not reduced fertility) compared to individuals that hatched from eggs in utero.
source: This treatment was lethal for mothers but did not cause any mortality of embryos laid ex utero. Yet, individuals derived from ex utero eggs developed more slowly and exhibited significantly delayed reproductive maturity (but not reduced fertility) compared to individuals that hatched from eggs in utero (Figure 15C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 15C and D.

claim: Larvae in utero at the time of stress exposure to a low concentration of acetic acid (1 M) were protected by their mother's body and produced as many offspring as animals in control conditions.
source: In addition, larvae in utero at the time of stress exposure were also protected by their mother's body and produced as many offspring as animals in control conditions (Figure 15C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 15C.

claim: Constitutively strong egg retention can enhance maternal protection of offspring by protecting a relatively larger number of eggs in utero when facing a sudden environmental perturbation.
source: Together, our experimental results suggest that constitutively strong egg retention can enhance maternal protection of offspring by protecting a relatively larger number of eggs in utero when facing a sudden environmental perturbation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of experiments testing offspring protection under various stress conditions.

claim: Prolonged egg retention will reduce the total time of external exposure of the immobile embryonic stage, thus likely lowering risks associated with diverse environmental threats, including exposure to predators and pathogens.
source: Prolonged egg retention will also reduce the total time of external exposure of the immobile embryonic stage, thus likely lowering risks associated with diverse environmental threats, including exposure to predators and pathogens.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that prolonged egg retention reduces external exposure time.

claim: The degree of C. elegans egg retention alters the interplay of antagonistic effects on maternal versus offspring fitness.
source: Taken together, our experimental results suggest that the degree of C. elegans egg retention alters the interplay of antagonistic effects on maternal versus offspring fitness.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing costs to maternal fitness and benefits to offspring fitness.

claim: Strong egg retention reduces maternal survival and reproduction.
source: On the one hand, strong egg retention reduces maternal survival and reproduction (Figure 9C, Figure 10B); on the other, by prolonging intra-uterine embryonic development, offspring may benefit from improved competitive ability (Figure 12) and protection against environmental insults (Figure 13, Figure 14, Figure 15).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9C and Figure 10B.

claim: By prolonging intra-uterine embryonic development, offspring may benefit from improved competitive ability.
source: On the one hand, strong egg retention reduces maternal survival and reproduction (Figure 9C, Figure 10B); on the other, by prolonging intra-uterine embryonic development, offspring may benefit from improved competitive ability (Figure 12) and protection against environmental insults (Figure 13, Figure 14, Figure 15).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 12.

claim: By prolonging intra-uterine embryonic development, offspring may benefit from protection against environmental insults.
source: On the one hand, strong egg retention reduces maternal survival and reproduction (Figure 9C, Figure 10B); on the other, by prolonging intra-uterine embryonic development, offspring may benefit from improved competitive ability (Figure 12) and protection against environmental insults (Figure 13, Figure 14, Figure 15).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 13, Figure 14, and Figure 15.

claim: Variable egg retention, as observed in natural C. elegans populations, may reflect genetic differences in the adjustment of an intergenerational fitness trade-off.
source: Therefore, variable egg retention, as observed in natural C. elegans populations, may reflect genetic differences in the adjustment of an intergenerational fitness trade-off.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined evidence of antagonistic effects on maternal and offspring fitness.

claim: In extreme cases of strong constitutive egg retention, C. elegans strains exhibit partial viviparity, associated with significantly reduced maternal reproduction and survival.
source: In extreme cases of strong constitutive egg retention, C. elegans strains exhibit partial viviparity, associated with significantly reduced maternal reproduction and survival.
evidence: The claim is supported by data on Class III strains showing strong egg retention, internal hatching, and reduced maternal fitness.

claim: Observed genetically variable duration of intra-uterine development in C. elegans aligns with past reports showing that transitions towards viviparity incur maternal fitness costs as observed for diverse invertebrate and vertebrate taxa with both inter- and intraspecific differences in egg-laying modes.
source: Overall, observed genetically variable duration of intra-uterine development in C. elegans thus seems to align well with past reports showing that transitions towards viviparity incur maternal fitness costs as observed for diverse invertebrate and vertebrate taxa with both inter- and intraspecific differences in egg-laying modes (Avise, 2013; Blackburn, 2015; Kalinka, 2015; Ostrovsky et al., 2016; Horváth and Kalinka, 2018; Whittington et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by the current study's findings and is consistent with previously published findings across diverse taxa (Avise, 2013; Blackburn, 2015; Kalinka, 2015; Ostrovsky et al., 2016; Horváth and Kalinka, 2018; Whittington et al., 2022).

claim: Given the nearly exclusive selfing mode of reproduction in C. elegans, there is expected to be none to very little genetic disparity between hermaphrodite mothers and offspring, indicating much reduced opportunities for intergenerational conflict.
source: However, given the nearly exclusive selfing mode of reproduction in C. elegans (Barrière and Félix, 2005; Lee et al., 2021), we expect none to very little genetic disparity between hermaphrodite mothers and offspring, indicating much reduced opportunities for intergenerational conflict.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the known selfing mode of reproduction in C. elegans and draws on established knowledge from previous publications (Barrière and Félix, 2005; Lee et al., 2021).

claim: Observed natural differences in C. elegans egg retention are predicted to reflect properties of genetically distinct (effectively clonally propagating) genotypes, likely resulting from adaptation to distinct ecological niches differing in nature, fluctuations, and predictability of resource availability.
source: Observed natural differences in C. elegans egg retention are therefore predicted to reflect properties of genetically distinct (effectively clonally propagating) genotypes, likely resulting from adaptation to distinct ecological niches differing in nature, fluctuations, and predictability of resource availability (Blackburn, 1999; Meier et al., 1999; Trexler and DeAngelis, 2003; Kalinka, 2015; Mueller and Bitner, 2015; Dey et al., 2016; Horváth and Kalinka, 2018).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed variation and is consistent with theoretical and empirical findings on ecological adaptation (Blackburn, 1999; Meier et al., 1999; Trexler and DeAngelis, 2003; Kalinka, 2015; Mueller and Bitner, 2015; Dey et al., 2016; Horváth and Kalinka, 2018).

claim: C. elegans exhibits quantitative variation in egg retention, with rare instances of extreme phenotypes at either end of the spectrum.
source: (1) C. elegans exhibits quantitative variation in egg retention, with rare instances of extreme phenotypes at either end of the spectrum.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding from the analysis of 316 strains.

claim: Both common and rare genetic variants underlie observed phenotypic variation in C. elegans egg retention.
source: (2) Both common and rare genetic variants underlie observed phenotypic variation.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from GWA mapping and identification of rare variants like KCNL-1 V530L.

claim: Strain differences in C. elegans egg retention can be largely explained by differences in egg-laying behaviour, such as the onset of egg laying activity and timing of the rhythm between active and inactive egg-laying phases.
source: (3) Strain differences in egg retention can be largely explained by differences in egg-laying behaviour, such as the onset of egg laying activity and timing of the rhythm between active and inactive egg-laying phases.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from behavioral analyses.

claim: Behavioural differences in C. elegans egg laying map, at least partly, to genetic differences in the sensitivity to various neuromodulators, indicative of natural variation in the C. elegans egg-laying circuitry.
source: (4) These behavioural differences map, at least partly, to genetic differences in the sensitivity to various neuromodulators, indicative of natural variation in the C. elegans egg-laying circuitry.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from pharmacological assays and mod-5 experiments.

claim: Modified egg-laying behaviour causing strong egg retention – linked to frequent larval hatching in utero – negatively impacts maternal fitness.
source: (5) Modified egg-laying behaviour causing strong egg retention – linked to frequent larval hatching in utero – negatively impacts maternal fitness, but (6) prolonged intra-uterine embryonic development may benefit offspring by improving their competitive ability and protection against environmental insults.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings on maternal fitness costs.

claim: Prolonged intra-uterine embryonic development may benefit offspring by improving their competitive ability and protection against environmental insults.
source: (5) Modified egg-laying behaviour causing strong egg retention – linked to frequent larval hatching in utero – negatively impacts maternal fitness, but (6) prolonged intra-uterine embryonic development may benefit offspring by improving their competitive ability and protection against environmental insults.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings on offspring fitness benefits.

claim: Variation in C. elegans egg retention may reflect variation in a trade-off between antagonistic effects acting on maternal versus offspring fitness.
source: (7) Hence, variation in C. elegans egg retention may reflect variation in a trade-off between antagonistic effects acting on maternal versus offspring fitness.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main conclusion about the intergenerational fitness trade-off.

claim: C. elegans egg retention is a quantitative (complex) trait: observed phenotypic distribution and GWA mapping indicate that this trait is likely influenced by multiple loci of small effect.
source: C. elegans egg retention is a quantitative (complex) trait: observed phenotypic distribution and GWA mapping indicate that this trait is likely influenced by multiple loci of small effect (Mackay et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the phenotypic distribution and GWA mapping results and draws on established knowledge about quantitative traits (Mackay et al., 2009).

claim: Large-effect variants, such as KCNL-1 V530L, occur but they seem to be relatively rare in C. elegans.
source: In addition, large-effect variants, such as KCNL-1 V530L (Vigne et al., 2021), occur but they seem to be relatively rare.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that only a small number of strains carry the KCNL-1 V530L variant.

claim: Variation in reproductive processes, such as self-sperm production and ovulation rates, contributes to observed variation in egg number in utero in C. elegans.
source: Although variation in reproductive processes, such as self-sperm production and ovulation rates, contributes to observed variation in egg number in utero, we also present clear evidence for natural variation in egg-laying behaviour and involved neuromodulatory processes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed temporal dynamics of egg retention and is consistent with established knowledge about reproductive processes.

claim: The genetics of the C. elegans egg-laying circuit has been studied for decades, and dozens of genes have been identified by mutations, which either reduce or increase egg-laying activity.
source: The genetics of the C. elegans egg-laying circuit has been studied for decades, and dozens of genes have been identified by mutations, which either reduce or increase egg-laying activity (Trent et al., 1983; Schafer, 2006).
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge from previous publications (Trent et al., 1983; Schafer, 2006).

claim: Some of the identified genes in the C. elegans egg-laying circuit encode ion channels regulating cell and synaptic electrical excitability, others encode components of G-protein signalling pathways that act in specific cells of the circuit.
source: Some of the identified genes encode ion channels regulating cell and synaptic electrical excitability, others encode components of G-protein signalling pathways that act in specific cells of the circuit.
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge about the molecular components of the egg-laying circuit.

claim: Many genes transmitting environmental and physiological signals via sensory processing are known to regulate C. elegans egg laying.
source: Many more genes transmitting environmental and physiological signals via sensory processing are known to regulate C. elegans egg laying (Schafer, 2006; Ringstad and Horvitz, 2008; Fenk and de Bono, 2015; Banerjee et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge from previous publications (Schafer, 2006; Ringstad and Horvitz, 2008; Fenk and de Bono, 2015; Banerjee et al., 2017).

claim: Recent research has uncovered an important role of muscle-directed mechanisms regulating egg laying through sensation of internal stretch mediated by egg accumulation in utero.
source: Recent research has further uncovered an important role of muscle-directed mechanisms regulating egg laying through sensation of internal stretch mediated by egg accumulation in utero (Collins et al., 2016; Ravi et al., 2018; Ravi et al., 2021; Medrano and Collins, 2023).
evidence: The claim draws on recent published findings (Collins et al., 2016; Ravi et al., 2018; Ravi et al., 2021; Medrano and Collins, 2023).

claim: This stretch-dependent homeostat directly targets vulval muscles and is sufficient to trigger egg laying when synaptic transmission is reduced or defective, for example, in the absence of HSN command neurons.
source: This stretch-dependent homeostat directly targets vulval muscles and is sufficient to trigger egg laying when synaptic transmission is reduced or defective, for example, in the absence of HSN command neurons (Ravi et al., 2018; Ravi et al., 2021; Medrano and Collins, 2023).
evidence: The claim draws on recent published findings (Ravi et al., 2018; Ravi et al., 2021; Medrano and Collins, 2023).

claim: Changes in muscle-directed signalling components in response to egg accumulation are likely key factors driving the evolution of C. elegans egg retention.
source: As indicated by our results (Figure 6B), changes in such muscle-directed signalling components in response to egg accumulation are likely key factors driving the evolution of C. elegans egg retention.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Natural variation in egg-laying behaviour may arise through differential activity of developmental genes generating variation in the neuroanatomy of the egg-laying circuit itself, for example as observed between different Caenorhabditis species.
source: In addition, we cannot exclude that natural variation in egg-laying behaviour may arise through differential activity of developmental genes generating variation in the neuroanatomy of the egg-laying circuit itself, for example as observed between different Caenorhabditis species (Loer and Rivard, 2007).
evidence: The claim is speculative and draws on observations from other Caenorhabditis species (Loer and Rivard, 2007).

claim: The only known natural variant modulating C. elegans egg laying is the major-effect variant KCNL-1 V530L, which reduces egg laying through likely hyperpolarization of vulval muscles.
source: Currently, the only known natural variant modulating C. elegans egg laying is the major-effect variant KCNL-1 V530L, which reduces egg laying through likely hyperpolarization of vulval muscles (Vigne et al., 2021), so that stimuli, such as mechanosensory inputs, are insufficient to trigger regular and successful egg-laying events.
evidence: The claim is supported by a previous publication (Vigne et al., 2021).

claim: Other unknown variants must cause the strong reduction of egg-laying activity in Class IIIA strains.
source: Our new results show that other unknown variants must cause the strong reduction of egg-laying activity in Class IIIA strains.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Class IIIA strains exhibit strong egg retention but do not carry the KCNL-1 V530L variant.

claim: JU2829 might carry a variant with effects like KCNL-1 V530L, whereas variants with distinct functional effects would explain reduced egg-laying activity in other Class IIIA strains.
source: This suggests that JU2829 might carry a variant with effects like KCNL-1 V530L, whereas variants with distinct functional effects would explain reduced egg-laying activity in other Class IIIA strains.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed differences in serotonin response between JU2829 and other Class IIIA strains.

claim: The detection of both strong and subtle strain variation in egg-laying activity indicates the presence of many different natural variants that modulate egg-laying circuitry in C. elegans.
source: The detection of both strong and subtle strain variation in egg-laying activity (also among strains within the same Class), as revealed by our pharmacological assays and when analysing the effects of mod-5(lf) in different strains (Figure 8), indicates the presence of many different natural variants that modulate egg-laying circuitry in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed variation in egg-laying responses to pharmacological treatments and mod-5(lf).

claim: Molecular identification of specific variants will be essential to explore how the nematode egg-laying circuit evolves at the intraspecific level.
source: Molecular identification of specific variants will thus be essential to explore how the nematode egg-laying circuit evolves at the intraspecific level.
evidence: The claim is a statement about future research directions.

claim: The likely ecological factors shaping natural variation in C. elegans egg retention are unknown.
source: The likely ecological factors shaping natural variation in C. elegans egg retention are thus unknown and we have not found any obvious links between the degree of egg retention and habitat parameters, such as substrate type or climate.
evidence: The claim is based on the lack of observed correlations between egg retention and ecological parameters.

claim: The likely ancestral (divergent) strains only very rarely exhibited a Class III phenotype, which could indicate that derived state of strong egg retention may have been favoured by the exploitation of novel microhabitats during the historically recent expansion of C. elegans reflected by globally distributed, swept haplotypes.
source: However, the likely ancestral (divergent) strains only very rarely exhibited a Class III phenotype, which could indicate that derived state of strong egg retention may have been favoured by the exploitation of novel microhabitats during the historically recent expansion of C. elegans reflected by globally distributed, swept haplotypes (Lee et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that most Class III strains have swept haplotypes and draws on previously published findings on C. elegans population history (Lee et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2021).

claim: The typical C. elegans habitat is highly ephemeral in nature, exhibiting extreme fluctuations in nutrient availability and occurrence of diverse abiotic and biotic variables, including stressors and pathogens.
source: The typical C. elegans habitat is highly ephemeral in nature, exhibiting extreme fluctuations in nutrient availability and occurrence of diverse abiotic and biotic variables, including stressors and pathogens (Frézal and Félix, 2015; Schulenburg and Félix, 2017).
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge from previous publications (Frézal and Félix, 2015; Schulenburg and Félix, 2017).

claim: C. elegans egg laying is known to be highly plastic, strongly modulated by subtle and very diverse environmental factors.
source: C. elegans egg laying is known to be highly plastic, strongly modulated by subtle and very diverse environmental factors, so that our analyses in standard laboratory conditions can only capture fractions of the complexity.
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge about C. elegans egg-laying plasticity.

claim: Diverse environmental stimuli (food quantity and quality, osmotic or hypoxic stress, pathogens, etc.) have inhibitory effects on C. elegans egg laying and long-term exposure to these stimuli will lead to strong egg retention and matricidal hatching.
source: Most prominently, diverse environmental stimuli (food quantity and quality, osmotic or hypoxic stress, pathogens, etc.) have inhibitory effects on egg laying and long-term exposure to these stimuli will lead to strong egg retention and matricidal hatching (Trent, 1982; Aballay et al., 2000; Waggoner et al., 2000; Chen and Caswell-Chen, 2003; Schafer, 2005; Zhang et al., 2008; McMullen et al., 2012; Fenk and de Bono, 2015; Vigne et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge from previous publications (Trent, 1982; Aballay et al., 2000; Waggoner et al., 2000; Chen and Caswell-Chen, 2003; Schafer, 2005; Zhang et al., 2008; McMullen et al., 2012; Fenk and de Bono, 2015; Vigne et al., 2021).

claim: Plastically induced egg retention and matricidal hatching by prolonged starvation may allow for nutrient provisioning of internally hatched larvae as they can consume debris stemming from the decaying mother, hence allowing for developmental growth in the absence of external food.
source: In particular, plastically induced egg retention and matricidal hatching by prolonged starvation may allow for nutrient provisioning of internally hatched larvae as they can consume debris stemming from the decaying mother, hence allowing for developmental growth in the absence of external food (Chen and Caswell-Chen, 2003; Chen and Caswell-Chen, 2004).
evidence: The claim draws on previously published findings (Chen and Caswell-Chen, 2003; Chen and Caswell-Chen, 2004).

claim: The existence of pronounced natural variation in C. elegans egg retention and egg-laying behaviour generates novel opportunities to dissect the molecular genetic basis of intraspecific variation in egg retention, providing an entry point to understand the proximate mechanisms underlying evolutionary transitions between invertebrate ovi- and viviparity.
source: The existence of pronounced natural variation in C. elegans egg retention and egg-laying behaviour generates novel opportunities to dissect the molecular genetic basis of intraspecific variation in egg retention, providing an entry point to understand the proximate mechanisms underlying evolutionary transitions between invertebrate ovi- and viviparity.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the significance and potential applications of the study's findings.

claim: In contrast to vertebrate taxa with intraspecific variation in egg-laying mode, such as certain lizards, the C. elegans model allows for rapid and powerful genetic analysis, for example through linkage mapping of natural variants and subsequent functional validation of variants by CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing in multiple strains.
source: In contrast to vertebrate taxa with intraspecific variation in egg-laying mode, such as certain lizards (Recknagel et al., 2021; Whittington et al., 2022), the C. elegans model allows for rapid and powerful genetic analysis, for example through linkage mapping of natural variants and subsequent functional validation of variants by CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing in multiple strains (Evans et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge about the advantages of the C. elegans model system and cites relevant publications (Recknagel et al., 2021; Whittington et al., 2022; Evans et al., 2021).

claim: Nematodes display frequent transitions from oviparity to obligate viviparity in many distinct genera, including in the genus Caenorhabditis, with at least one viviparous species, C. vivipara.
source: Nematodes display frequent transitions from oviparity to obligate viviparity in many distinct genera (Sudhaus, 1976; Ostrovsky et al., 2016), including in the genus Caenorhabditis, with at least one viviparous species, C. vivipara (Stevens et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge from previous publications (Sudhaus, 1976; Ostrovsky et al., 2016; Stevens et al., 2019).

claim: Evidence exists for the evolution of egg-laying circuitry across oviparous Caenorhabditis species.
source: Although evidence exists for the evolution of egg-laying circuitry across oviparous Caenorhabditis species (Loer and Rivard, 2007), the specific cellular and genetic changes responsible for the transition to obligate viviparity in C. vivipara have yet to be examined.
evidence: The claim draws on a previous publication (Loer and Rivard, 2007).

claim: The specific cellular and genetic changes responsible for the transition to obligate viviparity in C. vivipara have yet to be examined.
source: Although evidence exists for the evolution of egg-laying circuitry across oviparous Caenorhabditis species (Loer and Rivard, 2007), the specific cellular and genetic changes responsible for the transition to obligate viviparity in C. vivipara have yet to be examined.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Resolving the genetic basis of intraspecific variation in C. elegans egg retention, including partial or facultative viviparity, may shed light on the molecular changes underlying the initial steps of evolutionary transitions from oviparity to obligate viviparity in invertebrates.
source: Resolving the genetic basis of intraspecific variation in C. elegans egg retention, including partial or facultative viviparity, may thus shed light on the molecular changes underlying the initial steps of evolutionary transitions from oviparity to obligate viviparity in invertebrates.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the potential significance and implications of the study's findings.
